title: Fed holds rates at 3.75–4% in 10–2 vote, leaving a December hike on the table
excerpt: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on October 28 in a 10–2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favor of another hike.
content:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady on October 28, keeping the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4% in a 10–2 vote — a pause that comes less than a week before the November 3 midterm elections and after the Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September, its first increase in three years.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring another quarter-point increase immediately. In its post-meeting statement, the Federal Open Market Committee said economic activity was expanding strongly while inflation remained elevated, and that gathering more information would help determine the policy stance needed to return inflation to the Fed's 2% goal. Consumer price inflation stood at 3.7% for the 12 months to September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh described the internal debate as heated. "We just had a fairly heated debate internally, with serious and careful exchanges. I think we made the right policy decision at this time," Warsh said at his press conference, adding that inflation was still "too high" and the Fed had not yet brought it under control. He also announced that one scheduled 2027 meeting will instead be devoted entirely to broad monetary policy strategy, meaning one fewer rate decision next year.

Markets took the hold in stride: the S&P 500 closed up 0.28% at 7,744.0, while the yield on the U.S. 10-year Treasury note rose 2 basis points to 5.02%, reflecting lingering inflation worries tied in part to rising oil prices. Traders are now more confident of another quarter-point increase at the Fed's final meeting of the year, scheduled for December 8–9, according to CME FedWatch.

What it means here: a Fed hold does not freeze what Laredo borrowers actually pay. Mortgage and auto-loan offers move with bond yields and lender risk assessments as well as the policy rate, so households should compare the actual terms offered rather than assume borrowing costs stand still. The next decision point is December 8–9 — and fresh inflation data due this week will shape that debate.
